research_components.name: Size-selective mortality and the 'bigger is better' hypothesis
research_components.description: Meta-analytic and empirical evaluation of whether larger juvenile and larval teleosts have a consistent survival advantage over smaller conspecifics, critically examining the 'bigger is better' hypothesis against longitudinal data from natural populations.
research_components.explanation: Both papers present the same meta-analytic research programme reviewing 30 years of literature and compiling longitudinal survival effect sizes to test whether body size consistently confers a survival advantage in young teleosts, forming the core thread of this researcher's work.

research_components.name: Predation, conspecific density, and juvenile fish size structure
research_components.description: Field-based investigation of how predator abundance and conspecific density interact to shape size-frequency distributions of juvenile fish in nursery habitats, using long-term empirical data on Atlantic cod.
research_components.explanation: This paper directly tests the hypothesis that predator and conspecific density selectively remove smaller age-0 Atlantic cod in nearshore nursery habitat, using 15 years of historical abundance data to link individual size with survival outcomes.

research_components.name: Meta-analysis of glucocorticoids as population health indicators
research_components.description: Application of meta-analytic methods to evaluate the consistency of the glucocorticoid–fitness relationship across species and populations, assessing the validity of glucocorticoids as conservation monitoring tools.
research_components.explanation: This paper conducts a cross-species meta-analysis of the glucocorticoid-fitness relationship, quantifying sources of variation and questioning the widespread use of glucocorticoids as proxies for population health in conservation biology.

research_subfield_preferences.name: Larval and juvenile fish ecology
research_subfield_preferences.description: Study of the early life stages of teleost fish, including survival, growth, and the ecological mechanisms driving mortality during the larval and juvenile periods.
research_subfield_preferences.explanation: Both papers focus specifically on larval and juvenile teleost ecology, examining how predation, starvation, food availability, and conspecific density influence survival and size structure in early life stages.

research_subfield_preferences.name: Meta-analysis in ecology
research_subfield_preferences.description: Quantitative synthesis of ecological literature using meta-analytic methods to draw generalisable conclusions across species, populations, and study contexts.
research_subfield_preferences.explanation: Both papers employ formal meta-analytic frameworks—one compiling 76 effect sizes on size-selective survival and the other synthesising the glucocorticoid-fitness relationship across diverse species—demonstrating sustained use of meta-analysis as a core methodological approach.

research_subfield_preferences.name: Conservation physiology
research_subfield_preferences.description: Application of physiological measures, particularly glucocorticoid stress hormones, to monitor and infer the health and fitness of wild animal populations in conservation contexts.
research_subfield_preferences.explanation: This paper critically evaluates the use of glucocorticoids in conservation monitoring, directly engaging with the field of conservation physiology by assessing whether hormonal measures can reliably indicate population health across species.

research_subfield_preferences.name: Fish population dynamics and nursery habitat ecology
research_subfield_preferences.description: Investigation of population-level processes in fish, including size-selective survival, predator-prey interactions, and the role of nursery habitats in structuring juvenile populations.
research_subfield_preferences.explanation: These papers examine how ecological conditions in nursery habitats—predator density, conspecific competition, and environmental gradients—drive population-level patterns of size and survival in juvenile fish.
